title: Kate Tyndall, Dr Alison Ventress, Parents' witness statements

blocks.text: 1 December 2022
Baby G
CONTENTS
MRS KATE TYNDALL (recalled)
Examination-in-chief by MR JOHNSON
First witness statement of [Mother of Baby G] (read)
Second witness statement of [Mother of Baby G] (read)
Witness statement of [Father of Baby G] (read)
DR ALISON VENTRESS (recalled)
Examination-in-chief by MR ASTBURY
Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Housekeeping
Thursday, 1 December 2022
(In the presence of the jury)
Mr Johnson.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you, my Lord. Usually, we would start an individual case by reading the parents' statements.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: We are going to vary that today and do the sequence first, if that's acceptable, just because of printing issues, something as simple as that.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So could I call Kate Tyndall, please?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: MRS KATE TYNDALL (recalled)
Examination-in-chief by MR JOHNSON

My Lord, you will recall that we reviewed at an earlier stage, I think in the context of [Baby C]'s case, Lucy Letby's working pattern and put it against the indictment, and we're going to do that now and bring it up to date to [Baby G].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So if I could invite the jury to look at the indictment and ask Mr Murphy to put the shift pattern on to the screen.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: This is a composite document that covers Lucy Letby's working pattern between the beginning of June 2015 and the end of July 2016.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Is this -- I'm sorry, Mrs Tyndall, would you identify yourself for the purpose of the record?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I'm Kate Tyndall, intelligence analyst.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Is this your work, this document --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, it is.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: -- that we see on screen? Thank you.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: If we could turn the page figuratively, please, Mr Murphy, and expand June 2015 first of all. So we see that count 1 is the allegation of murder in respect of [Baby A] on 8 June. We see that that was the first of two night shifts so far as Lucy Letby was concerned.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Count 2 is an allegation of attempted murder of [Baby B]. The jury will recall those events happened overnight from the 9th into the 10th, so that night shift, that's the second in the block of two.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Count 3, over the page, is an allegation of murder of [Baby C] on the night shift of the 13th into 14 June, which we see is in the next block of night shifts.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Count 4, the murder of [Baby D] on 22 June, which we see is in the middle of the next block of night shifts.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Count 5 is the allegation of the murder of [Baby E] on 4 August, which we see, if we move on, please, so we can see there are a couple of blocks of night shifts on the 27th and 28 June, the 1st and 2 July; is that right, Mrs Tyndall?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Could we scroll down, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Sorry, can we go back? I've been asked to do the rest of July. There were no night shifts other than the two at the beginning of the month in July 2015.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So we move on to August 2015, please. The allegation is of murder on 4 August, which we see that day is the final -- the 3rd into the 4th and the 4th into the 5th are the two final night shifts of a block of four. That's [Baby E].
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Count 6, the attempted murder of [Baby F], which is the case the jury has just considered, which we all now remember. A TPN bag
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: was hung just after midnight, the 4th into 5 August, and that night shift would have finished at about 8 am on the 5th.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: We move on now to -- so if we look at the rest of August we see there are no night shifts for the remainder of that month.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: We move on to September. Looking at the indictment, we see an allegation of attempted murder, the attempted murder of [Baby G]. The date of the offence is 7 September and, as we will see shortly with you, Mrs Tyndall, those events happened towards the end of that night shift, which is the final one in that block of four, starting on the 6th, going into 7 September; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: So that's the context.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: If we can now, please, with Mr Murphy's assistance, move to the sequence of events, please.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Again, completing the context to an extent, that's count 7 to which you have just referred?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It is.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: But then of course there are counts 8 and 9, which both also are alleged offences of the attempted murder --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: -- of [Baby G] later in the month. So there are the three counts that we will be considering one after the other.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We will. And so that the jury understand, the way we are going to present this case, subject to witness issues, which we always have to take into consideration, is we are intending to deal with count 7 as an individual piece of evidence, so to include the expert evidence on count 7, and then to move on to counts 8 and 9, which we will take together, for what are probably obvious reasons, because the two incidents happened on the same day, on 21 September.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: All right, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So that's the plan as things presently stand, but of course always subject to alteration if we run into witness problems.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So Mrs Tyndall, going to the sequence of events, we remind ourselves of the fact that [Baby G] was born on 31 May 2015 at Arrowe Park, which is on the Wirral.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: [Baby G] was, as a matter of fact, the youngest and the smallest of all the babies in this case.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Can we go behind that tile, please, Mr Murphy?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby G]'s father's surname is [Surname of Baby G]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Her mother's surname is [redacted], if that's how you pronounce it.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: We see that [Baby G] was very, very premature at 23 weeks plus 6 days. She weighed just over 1 pound at 535 grams. Her delivery was a spontaneous vaginal delivery and she was in poor condition at birth, requiring ventilation. There is reference there to the difficulties that [Mother of Baby G] had suffered in pregnancy.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: We see also the Apgar score. There was no record at all at 1 minute. It was at the lowest at 1 at 5 minutes but had significantly increased to 10 at 10 minutes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: If we move on, please, Mr Murphy to the second tile. Do we then see, Mrs Tyndall, that [Baby G] was cared for at Arrowe Park Hospital for the succeeding 13 weeks and 4 days? In other words from her birth on 31 May until her admission to the Countess of Chester Hospital shortly before midnight on 13 August?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Thank you. So by that stage her nominal gestation would have been about 37 weeks, adding the 23 plus 6 to the 13 plus 4, there or thereabouts?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I'll go with your maths on that.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Very dangerous, but hopefully basic enough for even me to get right.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So we see a note to which there were contributions by Caroline Bennion and Dr Alison Ventress, relating to [Baby G]'s admission shortly before midnight on Saturday, 13 August.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Sorry, I say Saturday. It's a Thursday. I can't even read.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: On the screen it says Thursday.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: If we move on to tile 4, please, do we see a nursing note -tile 4, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Do we see Caroline Bennion updating the nursing notes on the computer at 05.08 the following morning, Friday, 14 August?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: My Lord, Caroline Bennion isn't giving evidence in relation to this case, so we'll deal with the note if we may at this stage.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Can we go to the note? This is your transplant, in effect, of what she has written in slightly more legible format. Could you take us through what you have produced there, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It reads:
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: "[Baby G] transferred from Arrowe Park Hospital for continuing care, and mum was booked into Chester Hospital. [Baby G] was delivered via NVD at 23 plus 6/40, weight 535 grams. For past problems and management please see medical notes. Currently [Baby G] is on CPAP, PEEP of 4 in 29-40% oxygen with good compensating CBG.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: [Baby G] has been on CPAP since 17/7/15 and has occasional desaturations.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: "[Baby G] is trialling off CPAP in ambient oxygen and manages 1 hour in two episodes daily. May be eligible to trial Optiflow. A PDA was detected but not audible on examination to today. [Baby G] will require a CUSS at 36 weeks and has mild dilation. Fluids are all enteral feed, 180ml/kg, 2 x 12, all OGT. EBM with Gaviscon and fortifier."
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Thank you. In that context, the CUSS is the head scan?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I believe so, yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: The OGT, the orogastric tube, so rather than going through the nose and straight down the throat, through the mouth?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: And EBM, expressed breast milk?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Can we move to tile 5, please? This is a continuation of the same notes of Caroline Bennion, made slightly later, an hour later. Would you read those for us, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: They're made at the same time, it's just this transposition issue (inaudible) amount of content:
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: "Mum intends to breast feed and is expressing well.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Pump offered but mum has her own to try first. [Baby G] has no ROP and is due a review for ROP. Referral to be faxed in the morning. First immunisations have been given on 1/8/15. [Baby G]'s medication is sodium supplements, diuretics, lactulose, caffeine, lactulose [again], Gaviscon and Sytron and fortifier. Baseline bloods obtained and a CBG. [Baby G] has had metabolic bone disease but is not currently treated. Mum and dad have been shown around the unit and given contact numbers."
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Thank you. Do we then move on to tiles 6 and 7, which are your summaries, aren't they?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. Just explaining that [Baby G] continued to receive the care from that point onwards until the point where the sequence starts at 02.00 on 06/09.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: And the next tile, which is tile 7?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Just saying this is where the detail starts.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Just to put this into context again, we've now moved from 31 May, which is [Baby G]'s birthday, to 6 September.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The allegation made against Lucy Letby is that it happened on 7 September, so we're at the beginning of the day before the allegation given the circumstances -- the circumstances giving rise to the allegation?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Thank you. Tile 8, please. I'm not going to go behind these, but do we have the standard observation chart, showing [Baby G]'s heart rate, respiratory rate and temperature --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: -- recorded at 2 o'clock in the morning by Valerie Thomas? This is a shift, we know from the fact that the tile is blue-edged, on which Lucy Letby was also working as a matter of fact?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Thank you. Tile number 9 shows some detail which I'd just like to highlight if we can go behind it, please.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: You have typed for us here what's contained on the tile itself. Notably, the first detail that you have transcribed is that this was the 99th day after [Baby G] had been born.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: She was being fed expressed breast milk with Gaviscon and a fortifier?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: The amount she was being fed is 45, presumably millilitres?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Presumably.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: The route, 35 of those 45 via bottle and 10 down the NGT?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: PU, do you know what that means?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think it stands for passed urine. And then a tick.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: There is a tick, which we can just see after the -- I didn't even see that the first time. And then a comment, "Demand feed"?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Anyone with babies probably knows what that means.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Thank you. Can we move on to tile 10, please? Are these more nursing notes, this time made by Valerie Thomas, concerning -if we go behind it, I won't ask you to read it out because Valerie Thomas will be giving evidence so she can deal with it herself.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: We can see for ourselves that that deals with the feeds and other related issues.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Go back to the carousel, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Do we then have a sequence of five separate tiles, being tiles 11 through to and including 15, which relate to various medications and oxygen that were being given to [Baby G]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: We see that each of those five tiles bears the name of Lucy Letby alongside that of [Nurse E]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: So to tile 16, please. At 5 o'clock that morning, have you put in for us the neonatal feeding chart?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: And also in the succeeding tile, the chart which records [Baby G]'s heart rate, respiratory rate and temperature?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Thank you. Tile 18. Have you recorded the fact that the night shift ended, the day shift began, and [Baby G] was handed over?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: I'm not sure whether -- it may be recorded on the information behind, it may be a new name here that we haven't seen before. Yes. Vicky Blamire was the designated nurse for [Baby G]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: We know -- I think Vicky Blamire is a band 4 nurse; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I believe so, yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: So going back to the sequence then, please. In tiles 19 and 20, do we have the hourly observations recorded?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Then in tiles 21 to 25, another sequence of five medications or similar prescription records --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: -- at 8 am? At tiles 26 and 27 do we have the hourly observations recorded?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: This time by Vicky Blamire?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Then at tile 28 do we have another new name, so far as the evidence is concerned at least, Dr Stephen Brearey, who is one of the consultants at the Countess of Chester; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: If we go behind that, please, Mr Murphy, do we see your typed version of his written records? And if we just click again, please, to see the written records, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Not the most legible handwriting, but it appears from that that Dr Brearey conducted an examination of [Baby G]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: My Lord, Dr Brearey will be giving evidence about this so I'm not going to go into the detail if that's acceptable.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Returning to the carousel, do we then have three records timed at 11 o'clock of fortifier, Gaviscon and oxygen being administered to [Baby G]?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Followed 3 hours later, at 2 pm, tiles 32 and 33, by the observations and the feeding record?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: At tiles 34 to 37, again -- well, slightly differently, actually, they start at 14.00 hours and conclude at 14.30, but do they record similar information to that which had previously been recorded, the administration of fortifier, Gaviscon, oxygen and sodium chloride --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: -- to [Baby G]? Thank you.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: We come next to tile 38. Is this Vicky Blamire's notes written at 15.37, so mid-afternoon, concerning the care given to [Baby G] from 8 o'clock that morning?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: If we just -- to put what we've seen into context, if we just go to the note, please. Do we see that there, Nurse Blamire essentially records similar information to that which we've seen in so many different nursing notes concerning the safety equipment?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: She then summarises the fact that [Baby G] had been fed?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: And there are references to some of the medications for which we have seen the prescription records?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Thank you. So going back, please, to the carousel.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Do we then come to the observation feeding charts at 5 pm?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Then at tiles 41 to 45, do we have five records of various substances being administered to [Baby G], being fortifier, Gaviscon -- well, actually, the fortifier is 5 pm, the others are after 6, so 18.17 through to 18.33, but for various medications including Gaviscon, oxygen, furosemide, spironolactone.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I don't know how to pronounce that.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: I'm sure others can do better than I can. Anyway, we'll hear all about it, I'm sure.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Finally, before the shift change, do we then have Vicky Blamire's updated nursing note?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: If we go to that. We see that there had been a recent successful bottle feed and [Baby G]'s bowels were open?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: That's the day up to and including the end of the day shift on 6 September. The event with which the jury are concerned on this count happened at about 2 am on this shift, didn't it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: So we're going to deal with events on this shift. Can we click behind tile 47, please, Mr Murphy? First of all, do we see there that the paediatrician of the week was Dr Brearey?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: As we have seen, he actually examined [Baby G]. There is the coincidence of the fact that he was also on call for the shift that we're about to examine.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: The registrar was Dr Alison Ventress --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: -- whose notes we have seen in other cases, but who we have not yet met. The night SHO was Charlotte Newton.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: The shift leader was either Ailsa Simpson or Christopher Booth.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: The designated nurse for [Baby G] on this shift was [Nurse E].
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: And Lucy Letby was also working?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Finally, the nursery nurse was Lisa Walker?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: I think a bit further down we have the map showing that that evening there were seven children working -- as patients in the unit.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: So seven children, four nurses, and we see the relative designations. At least two children in nursery 1?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: One was a child whose initials were RIH, for whom the designated nurse was Lucy Letby?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: The other child, AC. Her designated nurse was Ailsa Simpson?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: In nursery 2 was [Baby G], whose designated nurse was [Nurse E]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: There were two children in nursery 3, MC and IO --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: -- whose designated nurse was Lisa Walker?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: But there were also, as denoted in that box in the bottom right-hand corner of the screen, two other children for whom the designated nurses were Christopher Booth and [Nurse E] respectively?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: So just to put that into a slightly different format, [Nurse E] had a child in nursery 2, who was [Baby G]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: She had another child, and we don't know where that other child was?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Christopher Booth, who may or may not have been the shift leader, had a child, DB, whose location we don't know?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: And the other potential shift leader, Ailsa Simpson, had a child in nursery 1?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Going back to the carousel, please, at about the time of physical handover, do we see that, in respect of [Baby G], the administration of sodium chloride, fortifier, Gaviscon and oxygen was recorded in tiles 48 to 51?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: And that Lucy Letby was the co-signer for those substances alongside the designated nurse, [Nurse E]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Do we then have administration records on the computer for those substances, which are tiles 52 to 55?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: And they are timed either 2 or 3 minutes after the prescription records are signed and co-signed by the respective nurses?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: At 8 pm, so tiles 56 and 57, please, do we have the observation charts for [Baby G] --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: -- and the neonatal feeding chart?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: If we can go back to the observation chart, please, Mr Murphy, if you wouldn't mind. Just click on so that we can get an idea of the -- and the document itself.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So we're dealing with 6 September at 8 o'clock, which is the very far left of the chart. We can see that [Baby G]'s heart rate has been recorded, for the rest of that day, twice at about 160 or thereabouts; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think -- I just can't see the whole chart. I think that that's... If we go down the bottom, we can see the... So actually, it's the 8 o'clock in the middle of the chart where it's saying 7 --

blocks.text: The first statement is from [Mother of Baby G]. It's dated 26 April 2019 and she says as follows:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I am married to [Father of Baby G] and we have a daughter called [Baby G]. [Baby G] was born on 31 May 2015. When I was 9 weeks pregnant I bled and I thought we had lost her.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Obviously I didn't and things went okay with the pregnancy until 22 weeks when I started bleeding again.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: So I was back at the Countess and found out that my placenta was very low. I spent 1 week in the hospital, then went home for a day, and then straight back. I was 23 weeks then.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "My waters were leaking so they sent me to Arrowe Park where they just monitored me as I was only 23 weeks and they don't do much when you're 23 weeks.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: It was on a Sunday and I was complaining about stomachache and they were saying it was because of the iron tablets I was having.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The family stayed for a while and after everyone left I was still complaining about stomach cramps.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I was trying to sleep and I told the midwife I couldn't help it any more and I needed something to help me go to the toilet. I went to the bathroom and [Baby G] came out.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The emergency bell didn't work, I was pulling it and nothing happened. No one came. But something told me to stay there and so I was screaming and hitting the walls. Then whoever was next door came and I told them [Baby G] was only 23/24 weeks. They went for help and everyone just rushed in. I didn't even know whether she was a girl or a boy at first and when they said it was a girl I just said, 'Save [Baby G]'.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "They were trying to calm me down and trying to calm her down. But as they were putting wires on her she kept taking them off. She was only 1 pound and 2 ounces and she was just a little tiny thing, fighting them. So it showed that she was a fighter.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "During her time at Arrowe Park they had something like five discussions with us about [Baby G] not making it, but she showed the doctors that she was a fighter. She actually made good progress and there were no issues.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: They took brain scans all the time, particularly at 23 to 24 weeks, because premature babies have a lot of brain bleeds, but it all went well.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At the start of her time at Arrowe Park she was in the first cot in intensive care, but then she ended up in the fourth cot and that was like graduation because you can go to the high dependency unit after that. I think she was 7 weeks old when I was finally able to hold her for the first time.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I remember the day [Baby G] moved to the HDU because [Baby G] was smiling and was really alert with the nurse.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I would read to her, stuff like that, sing to her, and you could notice the difference in her when you did. It was just a case of her growing and getting bigger and stronger at Arrowe Park.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "By 12 weeks old she had done so well that they said she could now go to Chester. She was nearly full term when we got to the Countess, about 35 weeks, and she weighed about 4 pounds. She was there for 2 weeks then turned 100 days old. The nurses did a banner and a cake and I remember it was Lucy who was looking after her that day.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "We had visited during the day but when [Father of Baby G] and I were at home that night, the hospital phones us and told us [Baby G] had vomited but was okay. But when we got to the hospital she was in intensive care with all these machines and everything. It was such a shock to us and she looked like she was going to die.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby G] then had to go back to Arrowe Park again. We stayed in Arrowe Park for 9 days before she was as well enough to go back to Chester.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "When we got back to Chester she had to initially go into the high dependency unit for a day because they needed to see if she had any infectious or bugs. But after that we went directly to the second room. Then we almost got to the nursery, but [Baby G] got sick again and had to go back to intensive care.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby G] was much better when she got back to the Countess but it was then we noticed a difference with her. Her expression had changed after she had been sick and she looked different. They took a lot of brain scans but said she would just have little catches and would just be a little clumsy but nothing more.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby G] stayed on breast milk for 6 months. I did everything in my power to help her.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I remember an occasion at the Countess when Lucy told me she needed to take [Baby G]'s bloods as they thought she had an infection again. She said I should go and wait in the parents' room. That wasn't unusual for when they took bloods: the nurses would say, go out for a bit, then come back. I went for a coffee but something just pinched me and I decided to go back early. I just couldn't wait any longer so I went back to nursery 2.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby G] was freaking out and screaming and just looked so puzzled. Lucy was with another member of staff and both were trying to calm [Baby G] down but I can't remember who it was with her. They let me hold her in the end because that's the thing that calms her down, cuddles.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: [Baby G] went to intensive care that day.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "In total she ended up in intensive care three times after she got back to Chester. Every time she moved up to the nursery room, it seemed she would end up sick again.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "My normal routine was that I would spend the whole day with [Baby G] and then [Father of Baby G] would go in the evening and stay until about 12. At the weekend we always went together and stayed until 1 am or something like that.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I would always ring at 6 o'clock in the morning to find out how [Baby G] had been through the night and then I would phone at 7 or 8 in the morning to find out which nurse was going to take care of [Baby G] that day. It wasn't that I had major concerns, I just wanted to know who was having her.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "We just tried to take our time in the Countess day by day and [Baby G] finally came home on 4 November when she was 156 days old. She has now been left with quadriplegic cerebral palsy and has microcephaly. She is visually impaired and is fed by a GJ tube into her stomach and so is nil by mouth."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Second witness statement of [Mother of Baby G] (read)
My Lord, there's a second statement from [Mother of Baby G] dated 4 March 2020.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: She says as follows:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I have been asked about [Baby G]'s dad [Father of Baby G] and I feeding her while she was in hospital. I remember we didn't start bottle feeding her until we went to the Countess from Arrowe Park, but when she first got to Chester on 13 August she was still being fed through her nasogastric tube.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I can't recall who it was at Arrowe Park who showed us how to feed [Baby G] but they would let us hold the syringe of milk after they had filled it with the correct amount of milk. The nursing staff would measure out the breast milk I had expressed and they would always be the ones who would put the milk into the syringe. They never let us do that.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "We were never allowed to aspirate either. That was always done by the nurses in both hospitals prior to us being allowed to hold the syringe.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The way we were shown would be to hold the open syringe without a plunger in it and let the milk fall through just using gravity. We were shown how to hold our thumb over the end of the syringe and count to five, then remove your thumb from the end, count again for five, put your thumb back over and continue.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I was told that if you held the syringe too high then the milk would rush through too fast and potentially make the baby sick, so you had to make sure you didn't do that and that you held it around chest height. We would always be stood up when we fed her.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "It was only a few minutes of being shown how to do the feeding and each nurse would check with you that you knew what you were doing before they would let you hold the syringe. It was all to do with making sure the milk didn't go into the baby too quickly.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Although I can't recall who showed us at Arrowe Park, I'm pretty much it wasn't while we were in intensive care and it was only when we got to the HDU that we did it.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "When we moved to the Countess the procedure was just the same: the nurses would measure out the milk I'd expressed and they would fill the syringe and would often allow us to feed her. It wasn't all the time that we were allowed to hold the syringe though: it depended on which nurses were feeding her and how busy they were.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Lucy would never let us hold the syringe to feed [Baby G] though. She always held it and fed her herself.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "When [Baby G] moved on to the bottle, I was always the one to give her the bottle if I was there, which I always was during the day. She would be on three daytime feeds a day and then I'd always ask them to wait until about 8.45 am for the first feed as I would be in and would have expressed fresh milk by then. The nurses would still be the ones who measured the amount out though.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "After she was poorly and got moved to Arrowe Park, we arrived back at the Countess on 17 September and she was then fed through the tube again and not through a bottle, although we have a photo that shows no feeding tube, so she must have been back on the bottle by then and that's dated 25 October.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "It was again the nurses who did the measuring and filling of the syringe or bottle. We were only allowed to give it to her but not measure it out."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

I visited [Mother of Baby G] on the Sunday with my mum and sister-in-law, who was staying with us, and we left [Mother of Baby G] at the hospital between 8 and 9 pm and went home.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Around midnight I received a phone call from Arrowe Park Hospital to say that [Mother of Baby G] had gone into labour and the baby had come. The three of us -- me, my mum and sister-inlaw -- all jumped in the car and drove to Arrowe Park Hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Eventually one of the doctors came to see us. They told us [Baby G] was stable and that we could go and see her in the intensive care unit. Only [Mother of Baby G] and I were allowed into the room to see [Baby G] and [Mother of Baby G] had to be wheeled in in a wheelchair. [Baby G] was in an incubator.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby G] was born on Sunday, 31 May 2015. Her due date was 21 September 2015. We were told by the doctors that [Baby G] only had a 5% chance of survival. [Baby G] weighed 536 grams -that's 1 pound and 2 ounces -- when she was born. She was no bigger than your hand but she looked like a tiny person.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby G] was kept in Arrowe Park for 11 weeks. During those 11 weeks we were called in four or five times as they thought she was going to die. Her lungs were underdeveloped and she had ups and downs. We were told that once [Baby G] was strong and stable enough she would be moved back to the Countess of Chester Hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "After the first couple of weeks, [Baby G] was much more stable. The older she got, the more we thought she was going to make it. I did not pick [Baby G] up until she was 2 pounds in weight as she was so small. We were told that very early neonatal babies are prone to bleeds in the brain, therefore [Baby G] had regular ultrasounds while at Arrowe Park to check for bleeding. [Baby G] did not have any bleeds to her brain while she was at Arrowe Park and all her scans showed that her brain was forming normally.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "After 11 weeks, [Baby G] was stable enough to be transferred to the Countess of Chester. It was the nearest hospital to our home address and she was taken by ambulance. When we arrived at the Countess of Chester Hospital we went to the neonatal unit and a nurse came to the door and accompanied us into the unit. [Baby G] was in the high dependency unit room.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Our general routine whilst [Baby G] was at the Countess of Chester was that [Mother of Baby G] would phone the unit in the morning, about 6 to 6.30 am, to see how [Baby G] had been in the night and then she would phone again about 7.30 after they did the handover to see who was looking after [Baby G] that day.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Mother of Baby G] would go to see [Baby G] every day, arriving at the Countess of Chester between 9 and 10 am. [Mother of Baby G] would stay with [Baby G] all day. I would then pick [Mother of Baby G] up on my way home from work, about 5.30, and we would go home and have our tea together. I then returned to the hospital about 7 and sat with [Baby G] until 10 or 11 pm.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby G] spent the first few weeks at the Countess of Chester Hospital in the HDU (room 2). She had a hot cot and was on low-
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: flow oxygen. When [Baby G] was in the HDU at Chester I think she always had her own nurse. As time went on, [Baby G] moved out of the HDU and into nursery 4.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: In nursery 4 the nurses had to look after two or three babies each, however the nurses' station was right outside the door of the nurseries, so I felt confident to go home and leave [Baby G] in the care of the nurses all night.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I never saw anything that caused me any concerns about anything at the Countess of Chester Hospital or about any of the nurses or doctors. I never saw anyone behave unprofessionally or cause me any concern.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby G] stayed in the neonatal unit at Chester for about 2 to 3 weeks with no real issues during that time up until the time she was 100 days old.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "On the day when [Baby G] was 99 days old I spent the evening with her as usual in the unit. [Baby G] was in the HDU. She was not on that much oxygen, just low flow, but she was still in a hot cot. She had been fed and was settled so I left at about 10 pm. She was fine when I left.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I went home and went to bed. I then got a phone call in the early hours of the morning which woke us up.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: The call was made to my mobile phone. I think it was about 1 am or 2 am. The call was from the nurse who had been looking after [Baby G] that night; I think her name was [Nurse E] or similar. She said not to worry but that [Baby G] had vomited and aspirated and that she had to go back on the ventilator. She said there was no need to rush over to the hospital but [Mother of Baby G] and I decided to go straight to the Countess of Chester to see [Baby G] anyway.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "When we arrived, [Baby G] had been moved to the ITU.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I noticed that the nurses had put up a banner in the HDU for [Baby G] to celebrate that she was 100 days old that day.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "When we went into the ITU, they were putting [Baby G] on the ventilator. We waited most of the day and most of the evening for [Baby G] to stabilise. I think Dr Stephen Brearey was there at some point but I'm not sure if it was overnight or in the day.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At one point we were sent to the meeting room while the consultants did their ward rounds. After the ward rounds they decided [Baby G] was just about stable enough to transport her. We were told that [Baby G] had only vomited the once, but it was
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: projectile vomit. She had never done this before. She has done it since several times.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I was concerned because I thought that [Baby G] had drowned in her own vomit while the nurses were stood around chatting.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "We waited most of the day and night for transport to arrive. The female consultant with the glasses was with [Baby G] when the transport team came for her. She was transferred to Arrowe Park Hospital in an ambulance.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: [Mother of Baby G] and I followed her there.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "It was the early hours of the morning when we arrived at Arrowe Park so they let us stay in the parents' room for the rest of the night. It took a couple of further days until they were able to properly stabilise [Baby G].
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "When we had previously left Arrowe Park when [Baby G] was 11 weeks old she was on air up her nose, known as Optiflow or something like that. It forced the oxygen up her nose. At the Countess of Chester, before she vomited, she was on low flow. This did not force the air up her nose but still gave her oxygen. After a couple of days at Arrowe Park she did not need to be on any oxygen at all any more and they took her off the ventilator and weaned her off the oxygen completely. We thought it was brilliant, even better than before.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "However, I noticed that something had changed about [Baby G]. When [Baby G] was in the incubator at the Countess of Chester, before she vomited, I would speak to her in the incubator and she would smile at the sound of my voice and react. Once she had had the vomit, I could see that she was different as she didn't respond to my voice the same anymore.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Once [Baby G] was stable, we were told she would be transferred back to the Countess of Chester, but we had to wait for there to be a free cot at the Countess of Chester. [Baby G] was at Arrowe Park for another couple of weeks. The day before she was transferred back to Chester [Baby G] had an MRI. [Baby G] was then transferred back to the Countess of Chester by the transport team and, on arrival, [Baby G] went into the HDU.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At the time I asked a consultant if there was a virus or anything in the hospital as another baby who had been in the same room as [Baby G] at the Countess of Chester Hospital was also poorly. Her name was [Baby I].
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: [Baby I] had been transferred to Liverpool Women's Hospital. [Baby I] came back to the Countess of Chester either a day or two before or after [Baby G]. I can't remember which. The
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: consultant assured me they had not caught a virus and nothing was wrong with the ward.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "As time went on, [Baby G] improved and she was moved from HDU to nursery 4. However, there were a few times [Baby G] had to move back from nursery 4 to the HDU and on one occasion [Baby G] went back to the ITU. On this occasion I came to pick [Mother of Baby G] up from the unit and when I arrived [Baby G] was in the ITU. They were trying to cannulate her to give her antibiotics and she was proper stressing. They had been trying for a while. [Mother of Baby G] said, let me hold her, and when [Mother of Baby G] held [Baby G] she immediately calmed down. They were then able to cannulate her and give her the antibiotics. I am not sure if she was only in ITU on this occasion because HDU was too busy.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "On each occasion [Baby G] was in the HDU she would improve and be moved into nursery 4 before taking a turn for the worse and having to return to HDU again. We knew that once you were in nursery 4 and out of HDU or ITU you're only a few days away from going home. It seemed that every time [Baby G] was well enough to move to nursery 4 and was nearly going home something happened and she dropped back into the HDU.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby G] was in HDU most of the time she was at the Countess of Chester. Thankfully [Baby G] never had to go back on a ventilator again and, as far as I'm aware, [Baby G] never needed CPR while she was at the Countess of Chester.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby G] stayed at Chester until she was 156 days old.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: She was then discharged home. This was in November 2015. When she came home she was still only 5 pounds. Once [Baby G] came home she remained stable for the first year and a half to two years. However, [Baby G] missed some of her milestones and the doctors were keeping an eye on her head measurements as her head had not grown as expected.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby G] had an MRI at the Countess of Chester Hospital at about 2.5 years old. It was only after that that we realised the true extent of her brain damage.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I have seen [Baby G] projectile vomit on other occasions since this incident where she has covered the cot. I think on those occasions they were linking her projectile vomit to reflux. There have been several occasions since [Baby G] was discharged from the neonatal unit where she has had to go to Alder Hey Hospital for medical procedures and/or treatment. Last year, 2018, she had to be ventilated six times in 10 months. She also had to be ventilated the year before as well.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "In addition, she has also had to have numerous courses of antibiotics. However, she has had a good year this year so far and she hasn't been ventilated since July of 2018. This is probably because [Baby G] is now PEG fed. She is nil by mouth. She has actually improved her health as she is no longer prone to chest infections as she is not aspirating as much.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby G] is still under the care of Dr Brearey. We've kept under his care at the Countess of Chester as this is the hospital that is closest to us. [Baby G] has now been diagnosed as having quadriplegic cerebral palsy.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: She has level 5 cerebral palsy. She suffers with dystonia, which was causing her spasticity, which means she goes really stiff and can stop breathing or holds her breath. At first when this happened we thought [Baby G] was having a tantrum, but we now understand this is involuntary.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby G] also has microcephaly. Microcephaly is where her head is small for her age and her brain is not fully developed. [Baby G] is also visually impaired. I don't know what [Baby G]'s life expectancy is. [Baby G] needs 24-hour care. [Baby G] currently goes to school a couple of hours day. She has nurses that come to our home for a couple of hours to week to support us. The majority of her care comes down to [Mother of Baby G] and me."
