blocks.text: "Plan: to cannulate [so insert an IV cannula], start IV fluids."
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And take some bloods.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Okay. Just explain that to us, please. IV fluids, what is the purpose of IV fluids?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So because of the large vomits and the concern over what had happened, we'd planned to give her a rest from her milk feeds and to give her IV fluids to keep her hydrated and to keep her sugars up while we worked out if there was anything else going on or not.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: We've heard something of the types of IV fluids, what would you have had in mind at that stage?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So it'd just be clear fluids. It would usually, for a baby that age, be 10% dextrose with some saline.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Bloods? What does that mean, blood tests?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Blood tests, yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: All right. And then we've got a "but", so we'll go on to the next page, please. It would appear that there was some sort of intervening event at that stage.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: So do you recall being called away from your examination of [Baby G]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't recall the actual being called away. I do have a slight recollection of being in theatre and being called back again, but again it's slight.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: When you were called away, do you recall the condition in which you left [Baby G] at that stage?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So I'd previously documented that she looked better and back to her normal self. So that would be -- I would have been happier -- I was obviously happy enough to leave her at that stage and I didn't call the consultant right then, so I wasn't that worried at that stage.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Okay. So you have noted that she looked better?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: You were called away urgently. And the fact that you haven't asked for the consultant at that stage, can we conclude that you were happy to leave [Baby G] at that stage with the nurses?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. I think... I didn't think I would be away that long and then I was coming back to her to carry out my plan.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If I thought I'd have been away for a long time, I would have called the consultant to come and help, more for an extra pair of hands rather than needing the consultant.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Okay. Do you remember how long you were engaged with the other task?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not exactly. From the notes, it was less than half an hour before I was called back.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And do you remember being called back?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It was 7 years ago, so as much as I can remember something from 7 years ago, yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: You're obviously having some difficulty recalling. Do you remember making a witness statement in this case?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And have you had the opportunity to refresh your memory from it today?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Okay. Would it be of any assistance to do so again now?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can do.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: My Lord, a copy is just being obtained. I don't want this witness to continue to labour with a memory test if that helps and no one has any objection.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, the note goes on:
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: "Called out of theatre to say [Baby G] gone apnoeic and dusky."
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: So sequentially, it looks as though you made your plan as to what you were going to do, you couldn't put it into effect because you had to go to the delivery of another preterm baby, but whilst you're there, you are called out of theatre to go back?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Exactly, yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: I'm happy to go on with the note for now --
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Are you happy?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I can't add anything more to that.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: We'll see in due course if your statement adds any further detail.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: So clearly from the note you were called out of theatre. You told us about half an hour, you think?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Less than half an hour.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: So bearing in mind that you first went to [Baby G] at about 2.30, what time of the morning do you think you are now?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Are you able to say?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'm sure I've seen it elsewhere in the notes. But I can't remember offhand. I'm sure I've seen it elsewhere in the note. I think on Dr Brearey's note it says what time he was called in and that would put (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Would it help to look at Dr Brearey's note?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If it's for the timing, yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Mr Murphy, could we scroll through to the page after these notes conclude?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Bear with us a second, we'll see if we can help.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: (Pause)
It may be behind tile 85 if there's any difficulty, Mr Murphy, or thereabouts.
(Pause)
Again, as we did before, if you'd just like to have a look at that. Thank you.
(Pause)
There may be a little bit more further down as well.
It says here "Called in at 3.30", so it was around that time.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Look at the rest of the note and see if it jogs your memory in respect of any other treatment while you were present.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: (Pause)
So we can go back to your note, please, and the stage at which you told us you were called back from the delivery suite to see [Baby G] for a second time, this was, during that morning.
Yes. So somebody had come to theatre to say she was apnoeic and dusky, so I've written on arrival, her sats, her oxygen levels, were 50% in 100% oxygen, which is the most oxygen you can give.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Pausing there, apnoeic?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Stopped breathing.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Dusky?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Sort of purple/navy colour skin. Low oxygen levels.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Very poor colour?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Okay. And 50% sats, what do they tell you?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So it should be over 92, really. So very low oxygen levels.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: All right. So also on your arrival, you point out that [Baby G] is receiving IPPV. Could you tell us what that is, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That stands for intermittent positive pressure ventilation from the nurse. So that's using a mask on her, on her face over her nose and mouth. You have probably seen it on TV with a bag that you squeeze, but in the neonatal unit we've got a Neopuff machine, so you just press, put your finger on and off the top and it does the same thing.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: So help with breathing?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: But you note that HR -- is that heart rate?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: -- is okay. You note continues:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Took 5 minutes for sats to pick up."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Took around 5 minutes, yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Is that what happened, do you recall?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. That's what I've written.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: All right. And then "Moved to room 1"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Was that your decision?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Why moved to room 1?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So room 1 at Chester was the more intensive care room and I felt at that stage [Baby G] definitely needed a close eye keeping on her and likely more support with her breathing.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Okay. You go on to describe -- just tell us the description you place underneath the decision to move to room 1, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I have written:
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: "Pink and well perfused with mask CPAP."
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: So the mask that you use to give the breaths, the IPPV that they were doing before, once she starts breathing again you can continue the mask, to put the mask on her face, but without putting your finger on and off the top and that just gives her a bit of constant pressure to make the breathing easier, but she is doing the breathing herself at that stage.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: The manual assistance from the nurse has stopped with the button that --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: -- you described to us, but there's now a mask delivering CPAP; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's the same mask, so you just stop doing that (indicating) with your finger and hold it there.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Okay, all right. And we've heard that the idea of CPAP is to leave some pressure in the lungs --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: -- even when the baby breathes out to stop the lungs collapsing?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: All right. You describe [Baby G] as active?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: So on the face of it, are these positive signs, having collapsed in the way that you've -- you were told whilst you were in theatre?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Often when a baby has an apnoea, they might need some help to recover from it, but then they'll be -- once they've recovered from that apnoea then they'll go back to being active again.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And that was what you found with [Baby G]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: "Tried for IV access x2 unsuccessfully."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Tell us about that, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So I tried to insert a cannula or a drip, but wouldn't -- unsuccessfully on two occasions.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: What was the purpose of that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: To give the fluids and antibiotics that I'd planned to before I'd gone to theatre.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: So they hadn't yet started?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And in fact you were unable at that stage to --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: -- put a cannula into [Baby G] to start administering —
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So that's again -- [Baby G] was born at 23 weeks, so being 3 months old at this stage, it's not uncommon that they have very difficult veins by that stage.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Okay, all right. The next line, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes:
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: "[Baby G] then had a further profound apnoea and her heart rate went down to 70 and sats went down to 40."
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Pausing there, was that in your presence?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, 99%, yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: All right. Now, correct me if I'm wrong, but why describe an apnoea as profound?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So it's quite common for babies to have short pauses in their breathing, but a profound apnoea would mean that their sats dropped very low and their heart rate dropped significantly as well.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: As you put on the next line, the heart rate, although it was okay, when you first arrived, it had dropped to 70; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And the sats are even lower than they were (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: You made a note about perfusion.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Tell us about that, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So her perfusion had worsened, that's what I mean by the downward arrow. CRT is capillary refill time, that was 3 seconds. It should be less than 2 -- 2 or less than 2.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Okay. Next line, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So IPPV, as I said before, breathing for [Baby G] via a mask was started again, and a gradual improvement was seen again. So her sats started to come up and the perfusion also improved with that.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: So rather than leaving it on CPAP, the nurse goes back to assisting -- actively assisting [Baby G]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: You then, according to the note, made a decision to intubate?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Just explain that to us, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: She'd had at least two significant apnoeas in a relatively short period of time, needing intervention with the nurse breathing for her, so we can't carry on in that situation.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So I decided to intubate, so insert a breathing tube into her windpipe, so we could put her on a ventilator.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And the ventilator then breathes for the baby?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Okay. The next line, is that "and concerns", "plus concerns"? Is that the next line?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "And concerns re [about] abdo [yes] so not keen for CPAP."
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Is that another consideration for ventilation?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Slightly, yes. So sometimes if a baby has apnoeas, you can try them on CPAP with -- I know I said we can do it with a mask, but that's not quite as good as the proper CPAP although it's the same principle. So that is a temporary thing and then you put them on proper CPAP if you want to keep them on it.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So that would -- sometimes that can help babies who are having apnoeas, keep stimulating them to breathe, but the downside is it forces air into their tummies as well. So if you're concerned about their tummy being large already, you don't want to make it worse.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Was that a feature that was concerning you at that time, the tummy?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It looks like it from the notes. I think it was a secondary -- I think the decision to intubate was mainly because of the apnoeas but that was a secondary concern underneath.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Okay, all right. And then it probably speaks for itself, but is that:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "No intravenous so no drugs used"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Scroll down, please. Your note continues, just explain that first line to us, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Intubated with a size 3..."
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: ETT is endotracheal tube. So that's just giving the details of the size of the tube that was used and "8 centimetres at the lips" is where I fixed it.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: That's the length from the tip of the tube --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's the length from the lips to the tip of tube, yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Then you have made a note about bloodstained fluid.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Tell us about that, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It says:
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: "Bloodstained fluid noted coming up from the trachea or between the cords."
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: So that's the vocal cords.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Is that something that you saw whilst you were intubating?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Then we've heard that the capnograph is a device that changes colour to show carbon dioxide.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Carbon dioxide, yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Do we take it that the word "positive" suggests the capnograph was showing that (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, it changed colour, so it shows that the endotracheal tube was in the windpipe, yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And is that "good"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Good bilateral air entry."
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: So we listen to the lungs with a stethoscope and there was good air entry on both lungs.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: So the ventilation is working and it's working equally on both sides?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. I don't think she was connected to the ventilator quite at that point. We'd have still been -- that same device that -- we connect that to the breathing tube once it's in --
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- rather than a mask.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: All right. So we're still at the stage with the nurse helping?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Okay. Do you remember --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It could have been me.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Okay, all right. Do you remember any of the nurses that were assisting in this process?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Only from the notes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: You don't have any memory yourself?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: So you then noted that Dr Brearey's attended?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: From his note now that seems to be about 3.30?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And you've then made a number of notes. Could you just take us briefly through the following notes, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Vent settings" is the ventilator settings that we started [Baby G] on. So 18/5 is the pressures that we set and with a rate of 40 breaths a minute.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Then I've put -- FiO2 is the amount of oxygen we are giving to [Baby G]:
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: "Weaned down to 30%."
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: So she was in (overspeaking) reducing it so that's a good sign.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: All right, okay:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Good gas 30 minutes post intubation"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: What does that mean?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's a blood gas that we'd have taken as a heel prick sample from [Baby G] to look at her carbon dioxide levels and acid levels in the blood. So it was good, that means -- so we weaned the ventilation settings, so we reduced the amount of help the ventilator was giving her at that stage.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Are they the figures at the end of the line (overspeaking)?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So 16 (overspeaking) decreased to 16/5 and an arrow down.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: (Overspeaking). So from 18/15 to 16 stroke -- sorry --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Then comment about a large leak. Could you explain that to us, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So the tube is quite a narrow tube --
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- and they only come in certain sizes and obviously babies come in different sizes, so you go for what you think is the appropriate size, but sometimes the vocal cords, the windpipe, is a bit bigger than the tube so you get a leak round the edge.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: When you talk about a leak, is it a leak from -- which way is the leak going and what's it of and (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So the tube is in the windpipe, so we're pushing air down the tube and then coming back -- I guess it comes back up from the ventilator.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Does it come up the same tube?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: So where does the leak occur?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So it's near -- so the tube is usually about 3 -- 2 or 3 centimetres into the windpipe by the time it has gone down the mouth and the vocal cords. So it would just be -- it could be when you're pushing air into the lungs or out, it could leak out -- rather than pushing it into the lungs it can leak out into the mouth and... yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Okay, all right. But that's round the edge of the tube as it passes through the vocal cords?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Okay. But was it something that didn't concern you at the time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Um, no. So it's quite common to have a leak on a tube.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: If it's a large leak, that sometimes means we need to use higher pressures than we would if it was a smaller leak to compensate for it. But we had good gases, her oxygen requirement had come down, she had good air entry, as I said, so it wasn't causing her an issue at the time, so we left it.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Okay. Is that "IV vit K"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Tell us about that please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So:
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: "IV vitamin K given due to blood from the trachea."
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Is what I have written. So because of the bloodstained fluid that I'd seen coming up from the lungs, any unusual bleeding in a baby we tend to treat with vitamin K because all babies are born deficient of vitamin K and that's an important factor in blood clotting.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Okay, all right. So you have said the air entry is good, sats are good. Do so we read into that that, following Dr Brearey's attendance at 3.30, was there an improvement in [Baby G]'s condition?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I'd say so. She responded well to the treatment that we'd given her anyway.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Okay, all right. But then at approximately 5.30 you've made another note. Could you tell us about that, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So I said:
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: "She had a further profound desat, heart rate down to 60, sats down to 40. Taken off the ventilator and..."
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: I shouldn't use so many abbreviations.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: It's okay, just expand it to us (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: IPPV, as I said before, is breathing for [Baby G]. And the Neopuff is that piece of kit that they have in the neonatal unit instead of squeezing the bag. It does the same thing.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: So at 5.30 do we assume from that then that [Baby G] was still ventilated?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: So she would still be receiving ventilation in that way that you (overspeaking) invasive ventilation?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And you had good air entry on both sides because you checked?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And the capnograph was positive?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: But notwithstanding that, we can see that there's another, as you describe it, profound desaturation despite the ventilator?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: If we can scroll down, please, the next line repeats the situation with the capnograph. It's still positive --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: -- and there's still -- it says "okay". Is that...
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If the heart rate and the oxygen levels drop on a ventilator, there's a few things that we always look for. You know, things change minute to minute so we can't assume that if the tube was in a good place at 3.30 or 4 o'clock that it's still in a good place at 5.30.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So we'd look for a displaced tube, obstruction, anything that's obstructing the tube, a pneumothorax, so a collapsed lung, or is it something to do with the equipment that was causing an issue. Those are our four standard things we would look for.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: So "capnograph still positive" would indicate that the tube is still in the windpipe, it's not dislodged, and the chest movement still being okay would indicate again they've got air moving from the ventilator into the lungs, so there's nothing blocking it completely.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: If we go to the next page please:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "This time recovered slowly."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. She'd recovered slowly on each occasion so far looking back on the notes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Okay, all right. Just read on with your note, please, and tell us about this recovery.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So recovered slowly with -- doing the breathing for her, with the Neopuff, still via the breathing tube. But when we put her back on the ventilator, she desaturated again, so we'd have taken her off and done the IPPV breathing for her again.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So at that stage I wondered if it was a problem with the equipment that was causing it because we could get her oxygen levels good without the ventilator, but it was when we put her back on the ventilator this time they went down again. So I was looking at if there was an issue with the equipment.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: So fine when she's having assistance through the button device that you told us about --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: -- but once back on the ventilator, would deteriorate?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: So you query ventilator problem, we see the question mark on the left-hand side.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: What's the flow sensor, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So it's a device that is on the end of the breathing tube, connected between the breathing tube and the ventilator, and it talks to the ventilator to -- it detects how much is flowing through it, the flow sensor, and then it lets the ventilator adjust itself in response.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Pretty well what it says on the tin --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: -- it senses the flow between --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: -- the end, ie the baby, and the ventilator itself?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Okay. But then "whole ventilator changed"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. We changed the flow sensor and that didn't make a difference, so then we changed the whole ventilator to see if that would fix the problem.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Okay, all right. A comment about the large leak remaining, could you just explain that to us, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: As I said before about the leak, I've commented on the previous page there was a large leak. This was still the case.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Still there --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: -- but because of sats and the heart rate --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I didn't think that was causing the problems.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Okay, all right. So after this event is [Baby G] still ventilated with the new ventilator and the new flow sensor?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: But at 6.05 we can see another event?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: So this is, again, about half an hour later, does that sound about right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Tell us, please, from the notes what happened at 6.05.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So another profound desat with a drop in the oxygen level and heart rate and then I have written "Decision to reintubate". So from the rest of the notes that feels like I've covered every other base and it's not really helped, so this is -- we'll do that.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So it says:
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: "IPPV [so again the breathing] given via the breathing tube initially."
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: So the heart rate came up to 120, but the sats remained low at 50, despite increasing the pressure we were giving and giving 100% oxygen. So I think it was after that, the decision to reintubate...
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Just generally, we've heard about 2.30, moving [Baby G] to room 1.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Events at 3.30, 5.30, 6.05. Were you with [Baby G] at her cot side throughout this period?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Probably for most of it given what's happened --
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: All right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- or at least in the -- at some stage I'd have started to write some notes, I wouldn't be at the cot side but I'd be at the desk in the room. I think the initial note was started at 4.40, wasn't it?
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So at that time I would have sat down and started writing notes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Okay. So we've got, I think, to the ETT removed at 6.10?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Take us through what you found then, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It says:
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: "Thick secretions ++ in mouth and blood clot at the end of the ETT."
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: What, if anything, might those two features tell you?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So thick secretions was -- you know, phlegm or equivalent was what we call secretions.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Does the plus plus tell you anything?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Just tells me more than I'd expect.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Then a blood clot on the end of the tube. We saw some blood coming up from the lungs when they're intubated so there was some blood in the lungs somewhere that's caused that blood clot on the end.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Okay. Are you able to conclude it was in the lung or just at a point below the end of the ET tube?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Um... Windpipe or lungs, yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: I'm not --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: -- just --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And we can see again:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "IPPV via face mask given."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Then:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Despite jaw thrust and Guedel..."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Tell us about that, please. I'm not sure we've come across jaw thrust before.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's all right. So again, we were trying to breathe for [Baby G] using the mask now because we had taken the breathing tube out, so a jaw thrust is when you try and bring the chin forwards to keep the tongue out -- off the back of the airway. Obviously [Baby G] would be laying on her back at this point so it's easy for the tongue to drop back into the airway. So we lift up the jaw to keep it off the airway. And a Guedel is a little plastic tube that you can put in the mouth to do that for you, to basically lift the tongue off the back of throat.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Okay, all right. And that's all, is it, to make sure there's no obstruction to the airway?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: All right. On this occasion you've made a slightly different note about chest movement. Tell us about chest movement by this stage.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, we weren't getting good chest movement despite these actions that were taken. So we'd have -- it would have been me doing the breathing at this stage from reading that.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Okay. Would you do the jaw thrust and use the Guedel?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: But poor chest movement -- and do we see the sats have fallen?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Is that a very low figure?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It is, yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And the heart rate's dropped as well to 70?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: If we can scroll down, please. Had Dr Brearey gone by this stage?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. I'm not sure at which stage he went, but he wasn't there then.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: But we can see he was called in again, as you describe it, urgently.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And tell us please about the next entry, about the NG.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So:
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: "NG [nasogastric] tube was aspirated as the abdomen appeared very large and around 100ml aspirated."
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: So this is post 6.10 when things have taken a significant turn for the worse? You're trying to work out -well, you have taken out the ET tube and you have used the airway assister and the jaw thrust technique.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Tell us about the aspirate, please, what you can remember of it.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So it's quite common when you're giving the breathing support via the mask for their tummies to get bigger because when you're trying to force air into their lungs, you also force air down into the stomach as well.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: So it's quite common in that situation that the stomach would get bigger and you would aspirate air out of the stomach --
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Was it air?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't say 100% from that. I would think, yes, but I haven't documented it, so I can't say exactly.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: All right. Do you recall if -- well --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think I would have documented it if it wasn't air because that would be more unusual.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And can you tell us anything about the quantity, the 100ml, is that usual, unusual?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It is a lot but, as I said, we have been doing that, forcing air in, quite a lot.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: All right. Did that have an effect?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It says the sats gradually increased after this.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Okay. We can see you then re-intubated [Baby G] at 6.15, this time with a slightly larger tube?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And she received intubation drugs to assist?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. It's kind of like a mild anaesthetic, the intubation drugs. It knocks them out a bit.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And perhaps because of the slightly larger size we can see the next entry:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Tight fit (inaudible)."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Did that eliminate the leak that you had noted early on the shift?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, it should have helped, yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: All right:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Bloodstained fluid in oropharynx."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is this in addition to what you told us about before?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. So that would have been when I looked in the mouth to intubate.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: So you have seen it the first time you intubated?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: When you have extubated there's been a blood clot on the end of the tube, on the tip of the tube?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And then when you've intubated the second time you have seen more bloodstained fluid --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The first time I documented it was coming from the windpipe, from the trachea. This time I've said it's in the oropharynx, so that refers to the throat basically. So it's not necessarily --
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: That's my next question: what's the oropharynx?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: All right. That's more the throat than --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's just below the throat, yes. So it's not just the windpipe, yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: All right:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Suctioned below the cords but nil obtained."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Explain that, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So when I went to intubate her, I'd have passed a thin suction catheter through the vocal cords into the windpipe to suction down the windpipe.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Is this because of what you'd seen?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Because of what I'd seen before with the history of the blood clot, so I wanted to make sure there wasn't another blood clot or anything I could pull out that was sitting there before I put another tube in.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Okay. But "Nil obtained" does that say?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Okay. You then secured the tube at 8 centimetres again?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: A positive result on the capnograph?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And again is that good bilateral air entry?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, it is.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And (inaudible: coughing) I may have jumped the gun:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Clinically leak much better"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Okay. So what was your impression -- from the notes what's your impression of [Baby G]'s reaction to that intubation at 6.15?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So we put her back on the ventilator at slightly higher pressures and I have put she was in 60% oxygen but weaning, so she responded well again to being intubated.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Then are they the settings again along the bottom of your manuscript note?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, 20/6 and a rate of 40.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: A little bit higher than you had earlier in the shift, but same rate of breathing; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: We can carry on down the page, please. Tell me please which comes first. There's a -- we've heard this a sticker that goes on the notes --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: -- after an X-ray so that people can fill in what needs filling in and then it looks like there's some manuscript to the right. Can you say which came first?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Because it suggests the sticker because you've squeezed your writing over to one side. Okay, so if we look at the sticker first.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: We've got --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'd have looked at the X-rays as they happened but not filled in the sticker, so I would have filled in the sticker when writing the notes and that looks like I was trying to fit it all on one page.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: That's helpful. X-rays taken at 4.48 and 6.36; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: We have heard that you get the opportunity to look at it at the cot side.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Then do you get a better look once it has been -- are they still developed?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: They are put on the computer.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Put on the computer, okay. So you get to see it in more detail; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Okay. All right. And you've recorded:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "ET tube position is good, no long line or umbilical catheters"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: The NGT or the OGT, do you remember which it was, was in the stomach?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: It matters not if you don't.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, I don't.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And you've made a note about the lungs. Tell us about that, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So I've written:
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: "Chronic lung disease, patchy +++ bilaterally."
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: So we know [Baby G] was born at 23 weeks and was on a ventilator for a significant period of time at the beginning of her life. And chronic lung disease of prematurity is -- all babies born at 23 weeks would have changes of that on their X-ray.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: All right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We know she was still requiring oxygen before any of this happened.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So I would expect to see chronic lung disease changes on her X-rays.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: So that reflects what you saw on the X-ray?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: The answer to this have been implicit from your answer, but anything that stood out as unusual or concerning in that respect?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not from my notes with her lungs, no.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Okay. Move on to the abdomen. I think that's what "abdo" stands for.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It is, yes. I just put "generalised gaseous distension".
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: In a nutshell, what does that mean, please? What did you see that caused you to write that or what would you have seen to have caused you to have written that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So throughout her bowels lots of air in the bowels. So if there's a blockage or an obstruction it's often just up to a point and then you can't see any after that, but that just looks like you could see lots and lots of air but the whole way through.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: You have signed that, timed and dated that at 7.45 on the 7th. So coming towards the ends of your shift?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And we have to the right a plan. Does that indicate you discussed this with Dr Brearey?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Tell us what the plan was.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It says "pancuronium bolus", which is a muscle relaxant medicine, so it basically paralyses her.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And the purpose of that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: To try and get better control of her breathing.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So sometimes an active baby on a ventilator, especially a slightly older baby like [Baby G], would try and breathe against a ventilator.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So... That kind of takes it out of the equation.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Okay. "Gas in 30 minutes"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Explain that.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Just do a blood gas test so --
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Another blood gas test in 30 minutes' time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Is that "continue morphine"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, "Continue morphine at 30". 30 is the dose.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Is that nil by mouth?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Nil by mouth and IV -- intravenous infusion, so IV fluids.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And cefotaxime --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Cefotaxime is an antibiotic.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Thank you. And I suspect the last note speaks for itself.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Okay. That, I assume, would have concluded your shift that particular morning.?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And we've heard that [Baby G], soon after, went back to Arrowe Park for a period of time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think the next evening, yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Thank you. I have no more questions. If you could wait there, please.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: We haven't had a break. I don't know whether anyone wants a break or whether we just press on.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It's very warm, but that's just me possibly --
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Would you like a break? Yes. I think someone would like a break. We'll have a short break.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you. I should say, my Lord, I'm likely to run into tomorrow with Dr Ventress if we stop at the normal time. That would happen whether or not we have a break. I wouldn't be done, I think, in 30 or 40 minutes. If I see that I can be, I'll let your Lordship know.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Can I leave it to you? If it means overrunning by 10 minutes we'll do it, but if it's going to take us to about an hour's time from now then I think that is -- I don't know, presumably you've got clinical duties tomorrow?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'd prefer not to come back tomorrow if I could.

blocks.text: We'll see what we can do. I'll check with the jury if there's any handicap to them sitting until later. There's none from my point of view.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Nor from mine. But there are some preliminary matters beyond what we have dealt with already that I do need to deal with or at least raise with Dr Ventress and then I can -- just so your Lordship knows, there is more than just what we've dealt with -- and then I'll turn to the main material here. But if I can see that we can complete it without trespassing far beyond 4.30 of course I'll endeavour to do so.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I'll leave it to your judgement. I don't know how long the jury want, but we may be able to keep this down to
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: 5 minutes, this break, the shorter the better. Do you want a comfort break or are you all right?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We're not expecting you to remember the details of this, of course, but it's something you would have seen.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Thank you:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And it was one of the conditions or a condition that she suffered from; is that right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It really describes the condition?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: It could be called chronic lung condition, in effect?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's fine.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: There may be a copy in court. I wonder if it could be handed to you, Dr Ventress. It starts at page 1842.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: (Handed)
If I may be allowed, I'll direct you straight to certain passages in it, and you can see them and it will help. We're 7
years away from events now but you made the statement back in January 2018, so it was a little fresher in your mind then.
It's still almost 5 years ago.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: It is, isn't it? Well, in fact, this statement was made about 2.5 years after events, wasn't it --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: So a baby like [Baby G], she was relatively stable at the time that you were looking after that we're talking about, wasn't she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Relative to her overall condition?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And the fact is, stable as she was, a very small baby like that requires medical help, doesn't she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: One of the concerns at all times with a baby like [Baby G] is that of infection; would you agree?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Because extremely premature babies are at a risk of -always at a risk of infection and don't have the reserves to cope with it well, do they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Do you agree? We'll come back to this at the end of my questions, Dr Ventress, but by the time that [Baby G] went back to Arrowe Park after this, the understanding then was this was, in all probability, linked to infection?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And it wasn't considered out of the ordinary in that context, was it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, not really.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Perhaps just to help you with that, I don't want you to feel you have to agree or disagree if you don't want to.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If you look at page 11, please, Dr Ventress, page 11 of 12. Just look down about eight lines. It says:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "[Baby G]'s condition was improving..."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Can you see that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: "... prior to her collapse. She was still a very small baby that required medical help. There was no suggestion at this time that [Baby G] was going to be released from the unit."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And then this -- I'd asked you whether the view was it was infection, you have agreed and we'll come back to that. I was asking you whether this was considered something that wasn't really out of the ordinary in these circumstances and you agreed at the time the view was there was nothing out of the ordinary or notable about what had taken place?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, it was symptomatic of a severe infection.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Thank you. Just one other matter I'd like your assistance with before we turn to the events you've been telling us about. A medical matter, so I'm going to ask you. I'm going to ask Mr Murphy to put up the blood gas chart for [Baby G]. It's at slide 95.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Can we just scroll down the page, please?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm going to ask you, for a moment, to pause at the entries that we have for the 4th and 5 September, which are the penultimate lines. Do you see those, Dr Ventress?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: The second and third lines up.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: All right. We can also see an entry for 7 September, which is the time we're dealing with, but I'm just looking at the two before then. I don't know, Mr Murphy, whether you're able to include on this the title line, which has the units or the items that we're looking at, so we can see what they refer to. If you could pull that down I'd be grateful.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I know what they're referring to if it helps.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: I'm certainly not there where you are, Dr Ventress, so I need the help. We're looking at the second and third from the bottom. If one looks at the pH value -- we've got a little understanding of what to expect from blood gases here. On the face of it, with that pH, there's nothing remarkable, it's in the normal range, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: But do you agree, as we move from left to right, the carbon dioxide level is raised?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And the bicarbonate level is also raised, isn't it, for both of those?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. That's typical of a baby with chronic lung disease.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: I was going to come to that when we look at this. Where it says "base excess", which we know is the last one along, that's a little high, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: So what that tells us is that there is a kind of acidosis taking place in the baby, some respiratory issue that the body is struggling to deal with?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's completely typical for an ex-premature baby with chronic lung disease. They would often have a raised CO2 level, which their body then compensates with keeping a higher bicarbonate level and a higher base excess to compensate. So therefore the pH, as you said is normal. So they're not acidotic at the time because their body has compensated for it.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: So the kidneys adjust to make allowance for the pH, don't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And again, although the pH in itself doesn't indicate anything, when you look across all of that it's consistent with the chronic lung disease, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: That takes us up to the 5th at that point. I'm going to move to the events on the evening.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We noticed on the notes -- we'll look at those shortly -- we saw how it was that you'd gone to the unit at the start of the event and then you'd gone away because you had to deal with another baby and then you went back.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. So the children's ward and neonatal, yes. A&E doctors -- the A&E doctors would deal with, unless there's a particularly sick child.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Sorry, I wasn't particularly clear (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It was unusual that we'd have to go to A&E, so it's mainly children's ward and the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Children's ward, neonatal. Did you also cover the postnatal ward too?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. But again, it was mainly the SHO that would go to the post-natal ward.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: So depending on the number of patients, you may have quite a lot of ground to cover in the course of one evening?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Which is no fault of yours, but that's how you had to work?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Could you scroll down just to where Dr Ventress' notes commence? Thank you, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Just to assist with your recollection here, Dr Ventress, I'm going to ask you if you'd look in your statement at page 8 of 12. I'd like to go through the detail that you give there that lies behind what's in these notes. Can you help me with that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Just look at the top of the page. The best you could remember in January 2018 was that at the time you were called for the first time to the neonatal unit, you'd probably have been on the children's ward. That's the third line down.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: You received or you were asked by one of the nurses to come to review urgently [Baby G] urgently at 2.35 am; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Just carrying on, you go on to say that you would have gone straightaway to assist and review [Baby G]; is that right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: All right. I'm just going to read from about halfway down to help us see what part of this was reported to you and what part you looked at afresh. You say:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "I believe [you are talking about the nurses] one of them was [Nurse E]."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Can you see [Surname of Nurse E] in large letters?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: All right:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "I do know from my notes that Lucy Letby was on duty and so she took over [Baby G]'s care later on but I'm not sure if she was present when I arrived. According to my notes, and not something that I actually saw myself, [Baby G] had just had a feed around 2 am then had a large vomit just before the call. Again from my notes, the nurse aspirated the milk from [Baby G]'s stomach. [Baby G] did have an NG tube through her nose down to her stomach for her feeds. From the notes it says 'large projectile vomit' and her abdomen appeared to be a funny colour, purple and distended, it looked like she was uncomfortable, red in the face and needing more oxygen.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I would have been told this when I entered the room."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So does that help with whether that's something you were told or something that you saw yourself? Do you agree?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, it sounds like it from that, yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: "I cannot remember who would have told me. However, looking at my notes, it looks like it was a nurse called [Nurse E], but I may be wrong. I don't actually remember seeing any vomit but that doesn't mean there wasn't any."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Then you say:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Again, referring to my notes, [Baby G] had a large distended abdomen. [Baby G] always had a big abdomen and that in itself is quite common in preterm babies but this was actually bigger than I would seen previously."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So this now is beginning to note things that you could see; is that right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Again, according to the notes:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "[Baby G] was already on oxygen. She had been gradually being weaned off her breathing support during the weeks before this episode. [Baby G] had never been off oxygen but during this episode her oxygen levels dropped, so the nursing staff quite rightly increased the amount she was getting."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Then you refer to the fact that in the notes it refers to [Baby G] opening her bowels with a large watery stool?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Is the position that having attended the unit, having been called to attend, receiving the information that the nurses gave you about [Baby G] and then forming the plan as to what should happen, you were then actually called away before you could carry anything through yourself?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Right. So if we look at the bottom of page 6542, where it says "planned to cannulate IV fluids and bloods", and let's just go over the page, please, Mr Murphy, if we could, "but unfortunately delayed due to delivery of another preterm baby".
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Right. So does that mean that having been ready to do those things, you couldn't deal with it because you were called back to deal with the delivery of a baby in the maternity unit?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, so it'd have been next door in theatre, yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: All right. Can we scroll down a little bit further, please, Mr Murphy? Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You were called -- we see three lines down:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Called out of theatre to say [Baby G] had gone apnoeic and dusky."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: So having gone back to the maternity unit, you are then called back to the neonatal unit; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Mm.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Right. I have to ask you to say yes if you agree.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, sorry.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And your understanding is the time of that would be a little bit before you called Dr Brearey to attend?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It would be around the time that I called.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Round about 3.30, something like that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: I'm not going to go back through all the steps that you took, but there will be some items I wish to deal with.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Can I just move down to the section that deals with "blood from trachea". Rather, "bloodstained fluid".
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If we just scroll down the page. You summarised what was being done to deal with the desaturation and to assist [Baby G] with breathing, and you had taken the decision to intubate; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And you took that decision because of the two profound desaturations that had already taken place?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Right. Where it says "intubated size 3 ETT", can you see that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: You can see that, ladies and gentlemen. It says:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "8 centimetres at lips. Bloodstained fluid noted coming up from trachea between cords."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Looking at this, but you correct me if I'm wrong, is that something that you noticed after the intubation had taken place?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, during the intubation.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: During the intubation. And is it the case that it's not uncommon for an amount of blood to sometimes appear as a result of the intubation process?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Um... It's not uncommon to have some injury to the back of the throat and around the entrance to the windpipe, but it is unusual to have blood coming up from beneath the vocal cords because that's not an area that we would touch with the laryngoscope.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Right. This is something that you only saw in the course of intubating; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Had you intubated, and let me be clear, at the time you saw it, or do you not know --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: -- or can you be precise as to when you saw it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So I would have -- the only time during the intubation procedure you can see the vocal cords is when you have the laryngoscope, which is a metal thing with a light on the end, that you put down into the back of the throat and use to sort of lift up, so you can see the entrance to the vocal cords. So that's the only time during the procedure that I would see the vocal cords before I put the tube in.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Right. So you put the laryngoscope in?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: You can then see the cords?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Would you intubate if there was blood present?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, if she needed it, yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: It says a bloodstained fluid. So is that blood mixed with something, some secretion?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. As I said, I can't physically remember it, but from the notes it wouldn't have been pure blood, otherwise I'd have written that.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: All right.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Once you'd intubated [Baby G], did the ventilator work to begin with as far as you can remember?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Um... Yes, from the notes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And was there no issue, so far as you were concerned at that stage, with blood interfering with what was taking place?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And there's nothing that you've noted indicating any continuing bleeding or anything of that sort, is there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And that's something you most definitely would look out for if you thought there was a bleed; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: My Lord, I have endeavoured to move as expeditiously as I can through the material I have to.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: There still is a little further to go, maybe about 20 minutes or so, and I'm aware of the timing.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I apologise for any inconvenience to Dr Ventress or to anyone else, but I have to stop at this point given the time that we're at, I think.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Well, I was led to believe that it really had to be 4.30.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, and for that reason this is as good a point as any to stop.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Would it be more convenient for you to start at 10 o'clock tomorrow or does it not make any difference?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm only saying exceptionally we could do it if it's going to make --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No, it won't make a difference.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: We'll stick to the usual 10.30 then. All right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So that's it for today then, members of the jury.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: 10.30 tomorrow morning, please. Please remember, no research into anything or anyone related to this case and no discussion with anyone who is not a fellow juror when you're all together, so no discrete discussions between any of you. Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (In the absence of the jury)
Housekeeping
As before, don't talk to anyone about anything to do with this case. 10.30 tomorrow morning.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: My Lord, there's an administrative matter relating to my arrangements that I wish to raise with your Lordship. I can do that now.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Certainly, yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It relates to 6 December, which is next Tuesday.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: As the court knows, as my learned friends know, there's a --
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Well, I know it'd be very difficult for you to be here on 6 December. I'm aware of that.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It would be and I'm grateful that your Lordship is aware of that. I know my learned friends have sought to try to arrange matters to avoid anything that could be regarded of pivotal significance to be taking place at that point.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Now, in the way that fate can do these things, it seems that, were matters to run their ordinary course, the witnesses who the prosecution would seek to call on 6 December on this part of the indictment are Doctors Evans and Bohin, who are, as your Lordship knows, the principal experts for the prosecution --
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: -- and witnesses for whom I need to be present to deal with them in cross-examination.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Well, look, Mr Myers, I appreciate the difficulty. blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No, not at all. Bubbling on in the background, there are other things. It would potentially advantage Dr Evans not to be called on Tuesday. So in that sense, it would suit his personal convenience.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So there you are, Mr Myers.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm grateful for that. I'm not sure whether that means we'll be proceeding with other material.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: That can be looked at, can it, and see whether there's anything or not? I don't suppose there's much else, is there?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Can I seize the proverbial bull by the horns, my Lord, and put it this way? Those are the witnesses who would naturally fall into place there and I understand that's what the prosecution had wished to do and it may be that, certainly so far as they are concerned, that would leave it as a day when they couldn't call evidence and wouldn't be ready to proceed, in which case I'd be in a position of asking if we could not sit that day, which I regret having to do because I'm anxious for the matter to proceed as much as anyone else is. blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Don't worry, Mr Myers. If it means we don't sit that day, we don't sit that day --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm most grateful, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: -- providing it doesn't cause any undue difficulty to anyone.

blocks.text: No, it causes no problems from our point of view at all. Mr Myers has an important thing that he needs to do. We have lives as well.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: It's not exactly the same, but it's almost equivalent of being required to attend in the Court of Appeal, where you have to go and courts are told in trials they just do not sit on that day.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It happens. Not to worry. That solves that problem. If there are any matters that can be dealt with, not relating to the calling of evidence, that can be dealt with then, one or both of your juniors will be able to assist.
